ENT Clinical Note

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: 5-day history of cough and “cold” symptoms; no specific trigger or exposure identified.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Began over the weekend (≈5 days ago). Dry, hacking cough; rhinorrhea; myalgias; chills; intermittent headache. Symptoms stable/mild; no reported progression to chest involvement.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat: mild sore throat; no throat-closing sensation, no dysphagia/odynophagia, no voice change/hoarseness, no drooling.  
  • Nasal/ocular: runny nose; no ocular itching/tearing described.  
  • Airway/respiratory: denies stridor, noisy breathing, dyspnea, wheeze.  
  • Swelling: none of lips, tongue, uvula, or face.  
  • Ear/neck: no ear pain, hearing change, or cervical gland swelling.
- Relevant past episodes/treatments: none reported.
- Allergies: not documented.
- Current medications:  
  • Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  • Lisinopril – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  • Paracetamol as needed for current symptoms – dose/frequency not documented.
- Social context: Patient at home in secure/private location; no mention of accompaniment.

Objective:
- Oropharynx: mild posterior pharyngeal erythema; tonsils normal size, no exudate.
- Neck: no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy per patient.
- Airway/breathing: speaking full sentences; denies SOB; no audible wheeze/stridor noted.
- Observable swelling: none.
- Mental status: alert and oriented.
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Third party presence: none.

Assessment:
Suspected uncomplicated viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold).

Evidence summary: Acute onset (<1 week) of dry cough, rhinorrhea, myalgias, chills; mild pharyngeal erythema; absence of fever, dyspnea, or lower-respiratory signs; self-limiting course to date.

DDx reference (consistent with transcript):
1. Viral URTI – high likelihood; presentation classic.
2. Influenza/ILI – moderate likelihood; systemic aches and chills, but symptoms mild and afebrile.
3. ACE-inhibitor (lisinopril) cough – low likelihood; temporal association weak and rhinorrhea/systemic symptoms argue against.

Plan:
- Symptomatic relief: advised OTC “Night Nurse/Day Nurse” preparations (compatible with current meds); continue paracetamol as needed.
- Monitoring/Red-flags: seek medical attention if any of the following:
  • Shortness of breath, wheeze, chest tightness, or noisy breathing  
  • Fever or clinical deterioration  
  • Symptoms persist >3 weeks
- No prescription required today.
- Follow-up: contact primary care/ENT if red-flags occur or prolonged course.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing but expected elements: allergy list, smoking/alcohol history, temperature and full vitals, dosing details for regular medications, vaccination status (e.g., influenza, COVID-19), prior similar episodes, occupational/environmental exposures.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none noted.  
● Transcript quality: clear audio; minimal background noise; complete for main complaint but limited ROS and vitals.
